visible.summary:
Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction where the federal "LGBT extremism" designation first produced a criminal conviction against a commercial leisure venue. The Pose bar case (submitted to court July 2025 by the regional Investigative Committee) resulted in June 2026 in a seven-year sentence for owner Vyacheslav Khasanov, prison terms for two employees, and forfeiture of over one million rubles—the first criminal LGBT-extremism sentencing against a commercial venue in Russia (the first prison sentence under the extremism designation overall was handed down by a Siberian court in an organising case, reported January 2025, predating this one). The precedent establishes that a bar or club can be prosecuted as an extremist organisation, which is the scenario a foreign visitor walking into a commercial venue is most likely to encounter.

This is visitor-facing enforcement: the venue context (drinking, socialising) is exactly where a visiting trans person might interact with the criminal justice system. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. Comparable to Moscow (0.09), which concentrates raids and the first organiser prosecution; both represent active enforcement venues within the uniform federal law. Orenburg's specific finding—a seven-year sentence against a bar owner—sets the most severe commercial-venue precedent in the country.
visible.tangentialFactors: The case is prosecuted as membership of the 'international LGBT movement' as such - the precedent it sets covers venues serving gay men and LGBT people generally as much as trans people, and forms part of the enforcement backdrop any queer visitor shares.

sources.claim: OVD-Info (10 Jul 2025): Orenburg's Central District Court registered materials in Russia's first criminal case under the Supreme Court's 'international LGBT movement' extremism ban - Pose club staff, case opened Mar 2024, sent to court 9 Jul 2025.

Novaya Gazeta Europe (29 Jun 2026): Orenburg region Pose bar owner Vyacheslav Khasanov sentenced to 7 years plus 1m rubles forfeiture, manager Diana Kamilyanova to 6 years 3 months, art director Alexander Klimov to 2 years 3 months - Russia's first known 'LGBT extremism' convictions, concluded in the region.

visible.summary:
Daegu has hosted the country's second-oldest queer culture festival every year since June 2009 — organisers mark seventeen consecutive years 'without fail', run 'as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics', the 2025 edition under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased' on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro. Organisers cite a Supreme Court ruling on local anti-discrimination ordinances as confirming sexual minorities as citizens protected by the Constitution.

The festival draws a recurring, organised counter-mobilisation: in September 2025 a Daegu–Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer', gathering roughly 3,500 believers from some 1,600 churches from Banwoldang station along a 450-metre stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans, timed against the festival. For a visible trans visitor the result is a concentrated confrontational environment during festival week; the event itself continues to take place annually despite interference.
visible.tangentialFactors: The annual counter-mobilisation around the festival is explicitly organised against homosexuality (same-sex conduct) and 'sexual minorities' generally rather than trans status specifically - its effect on visitors is the confrontational street environment it creates, not any trans-targeted rule.

sources.claim: Korea JoongAng Daily (2025-09): Daegu Queer Culture Festival has run every year since June 2009 without fail; the 2025 edition drew an injunction bid from the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasure Committee, dismissed by the court — as were the 2022-24 bids — while police again restricted the march to a single bus-only lane and organizers framed the event as resistance to 'hate and discriminatory politics'. 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. For the record: the sharpest local hostility in South Korea — state-adjacent opposition recurring annually but judicially contained each time.

Kidok (Korean Christian daily, September 2025): a Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer' response to the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450 m stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans.

Wikipedia's article on the Daegu Queer Culture Festival (DQCF), the festival at the centre of this record: it has been held every year since 2009 as the country's second-largest LGBT event, a pride parade and film festival lasting a week or two and usually taking place in late June, and it faces standing opposition from religious groups, with an estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups forming a 'gay issue countermeasure committee' in Daegu to block LGBT events. The page records that such opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central Daegu street, and it carries survey context on national attitudes (Pew Research Center: 18% of South Koreans felt homosexuality should be tolerated in 2007, rising to 39% in 2013). Framework source confirming the record's claim of an annual festival since 2009 and a recurring, organised counter-mobilisation in Daegu.

No Cut News (English, 8 June 2026): the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters — comprising the Daegu–Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association — filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea (NHRCK) demanding a change of venue for the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, claiming the event is likely to infringe on public welfare; the group says about 34,000 people signed, which it calls unusually large for a single NHRCK petition. The petition cites the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's injunction request, a ruling that found the police notice restricting the event legitimate because Daegu's Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. It counteracts the festival committee's January petition against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act. Dated court-and-petition evidence that official venue restriction and organised anti-queer mobilisation over the festival continued into the 2026 edition, directly supporting this record's account of a confrontational environment around the event.

visible.summary:
Movilh-Biobío formally denounced (14 October 2016) what it called "brutal and illegal acts of discrimination" at the Hospital Traumatológico de Concepción, where a trans woman was interned in men's beds even though public policy and the legal duty to treat trans people by their chosen name and social sex required the opposite — the complaint was lodged with the Seremi de Salud. (An earlier version of this record cited Law 21.120 as the standard breached; that law took effect in December 2019, after the denunciation.) This remains the closest Chilean analogue to a facility-misassignment incident directly encountered by a visitor: an emergency-room or inpatient visit in Bío-Bío carries a documented risk of gender-mismatched placement. Separately, Concepción's municipality dismissed the staff of its Oficina de la Diversidad y No Discriminación during the January 2025 honourary-staff cuts (~100 workers), which LGBTIQA+ organisations called a "dismantling" leaving one person in post.

Bío-Bío held 5.89 % of the national case total in 2024 — third highest — reinforcing that the region's institutional failures occur against an elevated baseline of discrimination reports. Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.10 deviation driven by two concrete traveler-facing findings: the hospital bed placement (medical exposure) and the diversity-office dismantling (loss of local complaint infrastructure). Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), Bío-Bío is 0.06 higher: Valparaíso's problem is the volume of over half the national case load, while Bío-Bío has specific institutional incidents but a normalised share. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Bío-Bío is 0.02 lower: Tarapacá's finding is a judicial annulment that devalues trans life in theory, whereas Bío-Bío's hospital episode shows how that devaluation manifests in the care a visitor might actually receive.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Concepción diversity office served sexual-orientation and gender-identity claims together; its dismantling degrades complaint infrastructure for LGBT people generally as well as for trans people specifically.

sources.claim: Movilh Chile (14 Oct 2016): Movilh-Biobío filed a formal complaint with the Seremi de Salud (Mauricio Careaga Lemus) over the Hospital Traumatológico de Concepción, where patient Hanna Jiménez Carrasco — interned 28 Sep to 3 Oct 2016 — was placed and treated as male despite public policy and the legal duty to use her chosen name and social sex; the complaint alleged 'brutal and illegal discriminatory acts' by hospital staff.

Movilh XXIII annual report (Mar 2025, 2024 data): Bío-Bío held 5.89% of the national case total — third-highest of Chile's regions — with Concepción among the cities with the most documented incidents (5). This is the dataset basis of the record's elevated-baseline claim; no region-specific source covers the share figure, so the national report stays (rule 5).

visible.summary:
Movilh's XXIV annual report (March 2026) identifies La Araucanía as the region where reported homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — up approximately 150 % year-on-year — during a year when the national total hit a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1 %). The region's formal trans visibility is extremely low: only 157 people used the Gender Identity Law (21.120) for name and legal-sex rectification in its first three years, indicating a community with minimal institutional presence. Movilh interprets the pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ+ themes have less public debate, stating this "appears aimed at obstructing" equality work.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.07 deviation, trend-driven rather than incident-specific. There is no trans-specific Mapuche customary-law jurisdiction or documented state-implicated violence in the dossier; the indigenous-note is structural context within a region under prolonged security conflict. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), La Araucanía is 0.01 higher: Tarapacá carries a concrete judicial annulment, whereas Araucanía's finding is a statistical acceleration from a low base. Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), it is 0.09 higher despite the 150 % rise, because Araucanía's absolute share (0.72 % of national cases) remains marginal.

For a visitor, the practical implication is not a specific hostile incident but the trajectory: the fastest-rising region with the thinnest LGBTI support infrastructure and least public visibility means fewer allies, fewer complaint channels, and a deteriorating climate without institutional counterweight.
visible.tangentialFactors: The +150 % rise counts discrimination complaints on sexual orientation together with gender expression and identity; the homophobic (LGB) component drives much of the increase but shapes the same climate of hostility a trans visitor would meet.
visible.localsOnly: The 157-rectification figure measures residents' use of the civil-registry procedure under Law 21.120; it signals community size and institutional presence, not a condition a short-term visitor encounters.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Parts of La Araucanía sit within a prolonged Mapuche land-and-security conflict that affects all travellers and is not trans-specific; the finding above concerns the trajectory of LGBTIQ+ complaints, not the conflict itself.

sources.claim: Araucanía Noticias (24 Mar 2026): Movilh's XXIV annual report names La Araucanía the region where recorded homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — +150% year-on-year. The same report put the national total at a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1% on 2024), with 2025 alone accounting for 23% of all cases in the 24-year series.

Movilh XXIV annual report (Mar 2026, 2025 data): La Araucanía accounted for 1.96% of the national case total while ranking first in year-on-year growth (+150%) — the report's own regional tables are the dataset basis for both the rise and share claims in this record; the region-specific news article does not carry the share figure (rule 5).

visible.summary:
Ñuble registered a +300 % increase in recorded homo/transphobic cases in 2024, the sharpest percentage rise of any Chilean region, though from an extremely small base: Ñuble held only 1.44 % of the national case total. La Discusión's reporting of two historic gender-identity rectification cases in Ñuble illustrates how minimal the formal trans presence is in the region. The statistical alarm is real — the fastest percentage growth in the country — but the absolute numbers remain marginal, and no region-specific legal finding, institutional incident, or enforcement failure was identified in the dossier beyond the case-volume trend. A 2026 follow-up in the same paper reports homo/transphobic attacks rising a further 16.6 % in Ñuble in 2025.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.05 deviation, driven entirely by the rate-of-change signal. Compared with Bío-Bío (0.62), which is 0.05 lower, Ñuble lacks the hospital bed-placement and diversity-office-dismantling findings that give Bío-Bío a concrete traveler-facing institutional failure. Ñuble's evidence is statistical trajectory without a named incident. Compared with La Araucanía (0.65), Ñuble is 0.02 higher: Araucanía's +150 % is in the most recent year (2025) and is accompanied by the lowest gender-identity-law uptake of any region (157 in three years), painting a more sustained picture of emerging hostility with no institutional counterweight.
visible.tangentialFactors: Ñuble's case figures are Movilh's combined homo/transphobia series — the +300 % 2024 surge and the 2025 +16.6 % attack rise include homophobic (LGB) cases and do not isolate trans-specific events.
visible.localsOnly: The rectification cases are civil-registry matters for residents (birth-certificate/name-marker change under the national gender-identity law, and the waitlist for state-transition healthcare one interviewee describes); they evidence a tiny local trans population rather than visitor-facing services.

sources.claim: Movilh Chile (18 Mar 2025): the annual human-rights report (2024 data) records 2,847 documented homo/transphobic abuses nationwide, +78.7% year-on-year, 23.5% of all cases since the series began — and Ñuble tops the regional rise table at +300% from a 1.44% share of the national total, the sharpest percentage increase of any Chilean region.

La Discusión (11 Jul 2026): 12,669 people have changed their legal name and sex nationally since the Gender Identity Law (21.120) took effect (through 2025); the article profiles two historic rectification cases in Ñuble — concrete evidence of how minimal formal trans presence remains in the region.

visible.summary:
Metropolitana is the region of best and worst in the country compressed into one administrative unit. Ñuñoa approved the first municipal anti-discrimination ordinance in Chile that explicitly prohibits hate speech, obliges non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, creates a communal seal for good practice, and requires anti-exclusion notices in municipal buildings — a genuinely first-in-country institutional protection for a visitor in that commune. Vitacura's mayor declined to raise the LGBT pride flag on 17 May after a rebellion by Republican councillors, despite a prior commitment to Movilh. The ADM1 unit's internal spread (Ñuñoa vs Vitacura) is larger than most regions' entire deviation from the national score.

Metropolitana held 25.12 % of national cases in 2024 (second only to Valparaíso), but as the country's most populous region this share is roughly proportional. In 2025, Metropolitana was one of only two regions where recorded cases fell. The unit carries the strongest institutional depth in Chile: national-level courts, the largest civil-society infrastructure, the greatest concentration of trans and non-binary community resources, and the highest density of legal aid and complaint mechanisms available to a visitor who encounters discrimination.

Against the national 0.72, this is a +0.02 deviation, the only positive unit score. The Ñuñoa ordinance and the falling case count edge the region slightly above national; the Vitacura episode and the 25 % share pull the other way but are offset by proportional population. Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), the +0.18 gap reflects that Santiago, despite carrying a quarter of national cases, has the institutional machinery to respond, while Valparaíso's problem is density of incidents without equivalent counterweight.
visible.tangentialFactors: Much of the recorded-case load and the flag dispute concerns sexual-orientation and general visibility conflicts (public rainbow symbols, hate-speech counts covering gay and lesbian people) rather than gender identity specifically - relevant to how a visibly queer-presenting visitor reads the two communes' climates.
visible.localsOnly: Protective depth concentrates in resident-facing machinery - municipal tender clauses, communal seals, the region's share of legal-aid and complaint bodies - which a visitor can use only if they stay long enough to file; likewise the ordinance's educational and health-programme provisions.

sources.claim: Movilh Chile (15 Apr 2026): Ñuñoa's municipal council approved Chile's first anti-discrimination ordinance by nine votes to one — banning hate speech, obliging non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, creating a communal good-practice seal, and requiring anti-exclusion notices in municipal buildings; drafted by the comuna's Diversity and Non-Discrimination Department head María Fernanda Ulloa and endorsed by mayor Sebastián Sichel.

The Clinic (30 May 2025): the Vitacura municipality — after committing to Movilh to raise the LGBT flag for the 17 May anti-homophobia date — reversed under pressure from its republican councilors and refused to fly it, while neighbouring Santiago and Ñuñoa comunas participated; a named municipal-level retreat in the capital's affluent comunas.
